lesson_title: Toasties, Seashells and Airbags: Limiting Reagents and Purity
hook_text: Ten slices of bread. Seven slices of cheese. The cheese wins. Here's why exams love that.
clip_script: Toastie recipe: two bread, one cheese. Stock this morning: ten bread, seven cheese. Quick — what runs out first? Everyone points at the cheese, because seven is smaller. Wrong. The recipe eats bread TWICE as fast. Ten bread only demands five cheese — you have seven. So the bread dies first, the kitchen stops at five toasties, and two cheese slices watch from the counter. That's the limiting reagent, and it's the exact trap in every Grade 11 stoichiometry paper: the smaller number is not automatically the one that runs out. Only the ratio test decides. And this isn't just sandwiches. Inside your steering wheel sits 130 grams of sodium azide — a bar of soap's worth of solid. In a crash it runs its recipe: two azide give THREE nitrogen gas. Sixty-seven cubic decimetres of gas, a full pillow, in thirty milliseconds. Engineers sized that pellet with the same arithmetic as the toasties. Get the ratio right and the airbag catches your face. Get it wrong and it doesn't.
visual_style: Overhead of a sandwich station: bread and cheese stacks shrinking at different speeds, bread hitting zero first; hard cut to a steering wheel cross-section with a tiny pellet blooming into a huge translucent bag of gas.
mood: Snappy and surprising — a kitchen trick that turns out to be life-or-death engineering.
pacing: Fast quiz open, one beat for the wrong answer, the reveal, then the airbag escalation to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never fall for the smaller-number trap again.
